title: -15°F, No Heat Lamp: All 12 of My Hens Made It. Here's How
description:
Last January it got down to -15°F on my porch, and my twelve hens spent the night in a coop with no heat lamp and no heater. Every one of them made it. The secret isn't heat. It's keeping them dry and out of the wind. Here's exactly how I get my Indiana flock through the winter, what it cost me this year, and the one thing I'll never put on a chicken.

My winter list:
• Vents open up high, above the roost, all winter
• No drafts at roost level (check with a ribbon or a candle in a jar)
• Wide, flat roosts (2x4, wide side up) so they can cover their toes
• Water open and outside, away from the coop door (heated base, or swap two rubber pans)
• Feeder full; a handful of scratch on the coldest nights
• Deep, dry litter
• A shoveled path, straw on the snow, and a windbreak on the windy sides
• Collect eggs twice a day so they don't freeze and crack
• Cold-hardy breeds; small rose or pea combs resist frostbite
• No heat lamp

Frostbite: don't rub it, don't thaw it fast, keep the hen dry and watch for infection.

This winter's prep cost me $81: straw bales and a tarp for the windbreak ($45), extra shavings ($24), a humidity gauge ($12).

This is what works for my flock in Indiana. If a bird is sick, call your vet or your county extension office.
